title: The Second Skin
author: Alexandre Dias
excerpt: She found it while brushing her teeth. A small doubled ridge of something beneath her tongue, folded like a wet leaf. It was, unmistakably, skin. It was not her skin. It was, also, undeniably attached.

chapters.title: Under the Tongue
chapters.body:
She found it while brushing her teeth.

The mirror was fogged at the edges from her shower, and she had not put on her glasses, and so she was, in the first moment, only vaguely aware that something in her mouth was wrong. A texture. A small unfamiliar folding, like a wet leaf, beneath the tip of her tongue. She stopped brushing and moved her tongue against it and felt it move back.

She rinsed her mouth. She wiped the mirror with the flat of her hand. She put on her glasses. She leaned close and opened her mouth wide and lifted her tongue to look.

Under her tongue, along the small ridge of tissue that held it to the floor of her mouth, was a translucent fold of something that was, unmistakably, skin.

It was not her skin. She saw this at once, the way one sees at once that a hair on the pillow is not one's own — some minute wrongness of color, some too-fine texture, some quality of stranger to it. But it was, also, undeniably attached. It grew from her, from the pale wet flesh under her tongue, in a small doubled ripple like the edge of a stocking that had been folded back on itself.

She was Yui Nakamura. She was thirty-seven. She had been born in Osaka and had lived in Yokohama since university, and she worked, without complaint, as a translator of technical documents for a company that made industrial pumps. She had no complications. Her health was good. Her teeth were straight. She had, since she was a girl, avoided doctors when she could and cooperated politely with them when she could not.

She looked at the small fold of skin, and she thought, with the clarity that sometimes comes at the beginning of things: *this is going to change my life.*

She rinsed again. She spat into the sink. She looked once more. It was still there.

She turned off the bathroom light.

She went to work.

—

She did not think about it during her commute.

This is not to say she forgot. She was aware, throughout the train ride from Kannai to Sakuragichō, of a small foreign texture beneath the tip of her tongue, a persistent otherness in her mouth. But she did not think about it. She had learned in her life that some things were better not thought about while there was nothing to be done, and that the space between noticing a thing and being able to act on it was a space that could either be filled with useful attention or with a low, spreading dread, and she had always preferred the former.

She thought instead about a translation she was working on, a technical manual for a positive displacement pump that had been badly written in the original Chinese and now had to be badly written in Japanese and English in a way that made the badness look intentional. She had made her small notes. She had drafted her small letters to the Beijing office asking for clarification on ambiguous instructions. She had, by the time she arrived at her desk, forgotten the folded skin under her tongue almost entirely, in the sense that she was no longer thinking about it.

Her tongue kept touching it. All morning. Small unconscious visits, the way a tongue visits the empty socket where a tooth has been pulled.

By lunchtime the fold had grown.

It was now visible without lifting her tongue. She discovered this in the small mirror of the women's washroom on the third floor, where she went during her break to reapply her lipstick and where, because she was alone, she permitted herself to open her mouth and look.

The fold was thicker. She could see, more clearly now, that it was not a single fold but a doubled edge of some thin membrane, tucked and gathered against the underside of her tongue, as if a larger sheet of tissue had been carefully accordioned and pressed there to be stored.

She looked at herself in the mirror. Her lipstick was, as always, a color she had been told did not suit her. Her hair, which she had cut short at forty because her mother had told her to cut it short at forty, was three months overgrown. Her face was the face of a woman who had learned not to look at herself too closely, and who was, in this moment, looking closely.

She saw, in her own eyes, the beginning of something. She recognized it. She had felt it before, though not for a long time. It was the recognition one had when something one had been waiting for, without knowing one was waiting, finally arrived.

She thought: *I should call a doctor.*

She thought: *I will not call a doctor.*

She thought this second thought with such immediate and full-throated conviction that she was, for a moment, surprised at herself. She had expected — she supposed she had expected — to argue with herself about it. She had expected the two thoughts to sit in her mind for hours or days, weighing themselves against each other, the way rational thoughts about a possible tumor were supposed to weigh themselves. She had not expected the decision to be already made, on some floor of herself below thinking, the moment she had first seen the fold in the bathroom that morning.

She closed her mouth. She smoothed her lipstick with her fingertip. She went back to her desk.

She translated pumps.

—

That night, in her small kitchen, she began, very tentatively, to unfold.

She had eaten her dinner. She had washed her single plate. She had turned off the overhead light and switched on the small paper lamp above the counter that her mother had sent her the year she moved out, and she had made a cup of tea and set it on the counter, and she had gone into the bathroom and stood in front of the mirror and opened her mouth.

The fold had grown again during the afternoon. It now hung slightly beyond the edge of her tongue — a thin pale ribbon, the color of clean bone, catching the light. When she stuck her tongue out a little, it moved with the tongue, attached at its rooted end. When she pressed the tip of it with her thumb, it was cool. It did not hurt.

She thought, and this thought came to her not in words but in a sensation of certainty: *if I pull, it will come.*

She pulled.

She used two fingers. She took the pale edge between her thumb and index finger, and she pulled, gently, the way one might unroll a piece of silk that had been folded into a small square. She pulled for perhaps three centimeters, and then she stopped, because she had felt the smallest tug from within — a faint sensation, not of pain but of *attachment*, of something being drawn from a place it had been coiled — and she was afraid, suddenly, of what she might undo.

She held the length of skin she had drawn out. It was, now that she could see it flat against her palm, unmistakably a piece of tissue. Not paper. Not silk. Something living or once living, thin as tissue paper but with a faint fibrous structure, like the film that separated the segments of an orange. It was warm from her.

She looked at it for a long time.

She said, aloud, to her reflection: *what are you.*

Her reflection did not answer. The reflection's mouth, hanging open with the small pale ribbon trailing from beneath its tongue, looked back at her with an expression she did not entirely recognize as her own. There was, in the reflection's eyes, a small quiet excitement — not fear, not disgust, but the recognition of something long promised.

She tucked the length of skin back into her mouth. It went easily, coiling small under her tongue where it had been. She rinsed her mouth. She spat. The water was clean.

She went to bed.

She dreamed, that night, that she was standing in a room she did not recognize, and that a woman she also did not recognize was sitting in a chair at the far end of the room, and that the woman was, very slowly, unfolding something in her lap.

—

In the morning the fold had grown again. It was longer now, and the pale ribbon that had trailed from her tongue the night before was thicker, and there was a second fold visible behind the first, tucked into the pocket of tissue where the first had come from, waiting.

She did not go to work.

She sent a message to her supervisor saying she was ill. This was easy. She had not been ill in seven years, and had accumulated more sick days than she could reasonably use. Her supervisor sent back a formal message wishing her well and saying she should rest for as long as she needed, which meant, in the language of the office, that she should be back on Monday. It was Tuesday.

She sat in her kitchen with a cup of tea. She did not drink it. She sat with her hands folded on the table, and she looked at the tea, and she thought.

She was thinking about the fact that she was not afraid.

She was, in fact, curious. She was curious in the way she had not been curious about anything in a very long time. She was curious about what was folded inside her, about how much of it there was, about what shape it would take when it was fully drawn out, about what she would do with it when it was.

She had not been curious about anything in this way since she was a child, since she had cut open the small dead bird her cat had brought her when she was seven to see what was inside, since she had spent an entire afternoon in her mother's sewing room unpicking the seam of a doll she had already ruined, to see what a doll looked like from the inside. She had understood then, and had understood ever since, that she was the sort of person who preferred to know what things were made of, and that most of her life was constructed around not doing this, because the world objected.

The world, at this particular moment, was not present to object.

She stood up. She went to the bathroom. She stood in front of the mirror.

She opened her mouth, and she pulled.

chapters.title: The Length of Her
chapters.body:
By the third day the pile on the bathroom counter was as long as her arm.

She had been unfolding, slowly, over the course of two evenings and one long afternoon, and the ribbon of pale membrane had grown steadily as she had pulled — thicker, wider, more clearly the shape of some flat organic thing that had been folded and folded and folded again, the way a paper crane, if unfolded carefully, would resolve into a single square sheet. She had pulled a length that would have reached from her mouth to her collarbone if she had let it hang. She had let it hang, once, to see, and had been startled by how much of it there was.

The material was not solid. It was more like the skin that formed on the surface of warm milk — soft, membranous, faintly ridged with what she had begun to think of as veins, though they were not veins because they did not carry anything, or because if they carried anything she could not tell what. When she held a length of it up to the light, she could see through it faintly. When she folded it, it stayed folded. When she draped it over her arm, it lay on her arm the way a wet handkerchief might.

She had thought, several times, of what a doctor would do with this.

A doctor would take samples. A doctor would run tests. A doctor would send her to a specialist, and the specialist would send her to another specialist, and eventually a small team of specialists would decide that they did not know what she had, that there was no name for it in any medical literature, that the closest analog was a certain kind of teratoma, or a certain kind of cyst that grew inside the mouth in cases so rare that the literature contained only a handful of examples, none of which resembled hers. They would want to remove it. They would want to biopsy it. They would want to photograph it and interview her about it and, above all, they would want to *end* it — to reach in with their small clean instruments and clip the anchoring root and lift out the folded thing and place it in a bag and take it away.

She was not going to let them do this.

This decision, too, had been made below the level of thinking, on some floor of herself that had already known it and was only slowly informing her of it. She was going to see this through. She was going to draw out the whole of what was folded inside her, however long it took, and she was going to find out what it was.

She wrote, in a small notebook she kept in the kitchen drawer:

*Day 3. Length so far, approximately 45 cm. Width, approximately 8 cm. The material is warmer than the surrounding tissue. It does not hurt to pull. There is a slight sensation of relief when I pull.*

She underlined the last sentence.

—

The relief was the thing she had not told the notebook, at first, in words she could have shared with a doctor.

It began the second evening. She had pulled another twenty centimeters of the pale ribbon out of herself and was sitting on the closed lid of the toilet, with the length draped over her knees, catching her breath, because pulling for long stretches was tiring in a way she had not expected — not physically tiring but *emotionally* tiring, as if some small internal effort were required to permit the drawing-out. She had been sitting like this, staring at the small pale sheet across her lap, when she had felt the relief.

It was a specific relief. It was the kind of relief one felt when one finally, after weeks of dragging around a heavy bag one had forgotten was heavy, set the bag down. It was the relief of a pressure lifting from something one had not known was under pressure. It was located, physically, in her chest — not in her mouth, where the tissue was actually being drawn from, but higher up, in the small hollow between her ribs, where she had felt for years a low tightness she had assumed everyone felt because it had always been there.

The tightness had eased by perhaps a tenth of what it had been.

She had sat on the toilet lid for a long time considering this. She had reached up with one hand and pressed the small hollow between her ribs, and had felt, or thought she felt, the very faint slow motion of something moving deeper, some folded thing turning inside her chest to release another length of itself into her throat. She had felt no pain. She had felt only the relief, and, beneath the relief, the very small terrible pleasure of realizing that she had been carrying this for so long she had forgotten it was there.

She thought: *how long has it been folded in me.*

She thought: *how long has it been waiting.*

She thought, finally: *I have been carrying this since I was a child.*

She did not know why she thought this. But she knew, when she thought it, that it was true. It was a knowing that did not go through the ordinary channels of thought. It arrived, and it stayed, and it did not ask her to justify it. She had been carrying the folded thing since she was a child — perhaps always, perhaps since before she was born. She had been carrying it, and it had been pressing on the small hollow of her chest, and she had gone through thirty-seven years of her life with the pressure of it, and had believed the pressure to be the shape of her, and it had not been. It had been the thing folded inside her, waiting.

She unfolded another five centimeters that evening. She slept without dreaming.

—

By the end of the third day she began to think about what to *do* with what she had drawn out.

She could not, obviously, keep leaving it draped across the bathroom counter. It was already beginning to dry at the edges where it had been exposed to the air for too long, and to curl at the corners. She had learned by experiment that if she kept it damp — she had begun to lay a wet washcloth over it during the day — it stayed pliant and warm. If she let it dry, it began to stiffen and pucker.

She fetched, from the bottom of her wardrobe, an empty shirt box her mother had sent her at New Year's with a scarf in it. She lined the box with a wet towel. She lifted the length of unfolded skin from the counter, carefully, gathering it in her two hands, and laid it in the box. It fit, folded loosely on itself. She placed a second damp towel over it. She closed the lid.

She wrote in the notebook:

*Day 3, evening. Approx. 65 cm now. Stored in box under bathroom sink.*

She looked at what she had written. She read it again. She thought about how, if a friend had come to visit — she did not have friends who came to visit, but she thought about it as a hypothetical, because she had learned to check her own behavior against the reactions imagined others would have — if a friend had come to visit and had found a box under her bathroom sink containing a damp folded length of pale skin, the friend would have called an ambulance. She would have been taken away. The skin would have been taken away.

She thought about this without alarm. She thought about it as a fact she had to account for, the way one had to account for the fact that certain kinds of mushrooms grew only in secret. She was going to have to be discreet. She was going to have to prepare, before very long, for the possibility that she would not be able to leave her flat at all until this was over — that the length of what was folded inside her might, in the end, exceed the amount she could reasonably conceal.

She sat on the edge of her bed in the small yellow light of her paper lamp, and she made a small list.

*Do not let anyone in.*

*Do not answer the door.*

*Do not answer calls from Mother.*

*Buy food for two weeks.*

*Buy more towels.*

She looked at the list. She added:

*Do not stop.*

—

On the fourth day the ribbon began to change.

It became slightly denser. The membrane thickened, and the pale color deepened by a shade, and when she held the newest length up to the light she could see, faintly, patterns in it — small darker lines that formed a shape she could not quite resolve, the way the pattern of a wallpaper only became clear when one stepped back from the wall.

She held a length across her palm and turned her hand this way and that under the bathroom light.

The patterns were, she thought, familiar.

She could not, at first, place them. They were not writing. They were not any shape she could name. But they belonged to something she knew. She had seen these patterns somewhere. Recently.

She stared at them for a long time before she recognized them.

They were the shape of the veins on the back of her own hand.

She looked at the length of skin in her palm. She looked at the back of her own hand. She lifted the length of skin so that it fell over the back of her hand, and the pale patterns aligned, not exactly, but by *kind* — the same branching, the same wandering, the same small delicate topology of vessels.

She stood very still.

She said, aloud, in the small bathroom, to no one, the thing she had understood:

*I am unfolding myself.*

—

She sat down on the bathroom floor.

She sat with her back against the wall and her knees drawn up, and she held the length of pale skin in her hands, and she looked at it for a long time.

She thought about the child she had been.

She had been a strange child. Her mother had told her this, without meaning to be unkind, many times. She had been the sort of child who did not smile at strangers. She had been the sort of child who preferred, given the option, to be alone in a room with a book than to be with other children. She had been quiet. She had been observant. She had had a small precise interior life that she had told to no one, because when she had once, at seven, tried to tell her mother about a dream she had had, her mother had listened with the expression adults used when they were being patient with something they did not understand and did not want to, and Yui had learned then that the interior life was a thing one kept.

She had grown up. She had done well in school. She had gone to university, and then to work, and had, over time, become a woman about whom other women said, kindly, *she is very calm*, and *she has such an even temperament*, and *nothing seems to bother her.*

Nothing had bothered her. She had understood, over the years, that most things did not bother her because she had, at some point in girlhood, folded them very small and put them somewhere. She had understood that this was what she did. She had not thought about what she did with them once they were folded. She had assumed, in the way one assumes about one's own interior processes, that they went away. She had assumed that they dissolved, or that they were digested, or that they simply ceased to exist once she had folded them small enough.

She had not, at any point in her life, assumed that they were being kept.

She looked at the length of pale skin in her hands.

She saw, now, that she had been assuming wrong.

She stood up. She washed her face. She looked at herself in the mirror. Her reflection looked back at her with the small quiet excitement of the second morning, still there, undiminished.

She opened her mouth.

She reached in with her thumb and forefinger.

She kept pulling.

chapters.title: The Shape
chapters.body:
It took eleven more days.

The exact count is written in the small notebook, which she kept faithfully, in the same neat backward-leaning hand she used for her translations of pump specifications, on the same lined paper her mother had sent her boxes of at university that she had never finished using. Day 5. Day 6. Day 7. Small entries. Lengths. Widths. Notes on the character of the material. On day 8 the material changed again, thickening further, and she noted that the darker patterns had become more definite, not vein-shapes now but something more like handwriting, a language she could not read.

On day 10 she stopped pulling for a full twenty-four hours. She had, she wrote, become tired. Not physically tired but the other kind. Some part of her had needed to rest before it could continue, and she had rested, sitting in her small kitchen with the box beside her on the table, the folded weight of what she had drawn out so far still under its damp towel, the whole flat quiet in the way that only her flat could be quiet, because she had not answered the door in seven days and had disconnected the telephone on the third.

On day 11 she started again.

By day 14 the material coming out was no longer flat.

She noticed this in the small hours of a Thursday morning. She had been drawing out a long length by candlelight — the electric light in the bathroom had become too much, and she had begun, in the evenings, to work by a single candle, because the candle made the whole procedure feel more like something she was doing carefully than something she was doing at all — and she had felt, as she pulled, a change in the sensation of the material passing between her fingers. It was no longer smooth. There was a thickness at one edge of it. A small firm spine.

She held the newest length up to the candle.

It had, along one long edge, a strip of what she could only describe as the beginning of something else. A small doubled ridge. A fold within the fold. As if what had been coming out until now had been the outer layer of something, and she was now beginning to reach the layer beneath.

She sat down on the edge of the tub.

She sat for a long time.

She thought about stopping.

She thought about this seriously, in a way she had not thought about stopping since the first morning. She had, she realized, been assuming that the folded thing inside her had a definite end — that it was, however large, a finite object, and that she would eventually reach its edge, and that whatever it was would then be *out*, in the box under the sink, in the world, and she would look at it and know it, and that would be the end.

She had not seriously considered the possibility that it went deeper. That the flat layer she had been drawing out for two weeks was itself only the surface of some further folded object, and that beneath it there might be another layer, and another, and another, and that the shape of what was inside her might, in fact, have no edge at all.

She sat and considered this.

She thought about her mother.

Her mother would be calling. Her mother would have called many times by now, and left many messages on the disconnected telephone, and had probably by now called Yui's supervisor, and would soon call the police, and Yui would eventually have to answer someone. She would eventually have to open her door. She would eventually have to be discovered.

She did not know what she would say.

She thought, with a small clarity that came from being very tired: *I have to finish before they find me.*

She stood up. She rinsed the length of new material she had been holding. She laid it in the box. She looked at the box.

The box was, by now, insufficient. She had begun, on day 10, transferring what she pulled to a large plastic storage bin she had bought from the convenience store on day 3 when she had gone out for the last time to buy food. The bin was in her bedroom, under her bed. She had lined it with wet towels, and she kept adding lengths, and it was, now, more than half full — a slow settled pile of pale folded material, damp and warm and slightly luminous in the low light, that had, she realized when she looked at it, taken on, in aggregate, a certain shape.

She had thought, at first, that it was only the shape of a pile. She had thought that any large soft folded material would settle into that shape when left in a bin. She had not, until day 14, noticed that the pile had begun to have a *form* — that the corners of it were not random, that the folds at its top were arranged in a way that was, if not exactly deliberate, then not exactly not deliberate either.

She stood in her bedroom and looked at the pile in the bin, and she saw that it was, unmistakably, in the shape of a person.

Not a person. The shape of a person. The way a pile of clothes on a chair, from a certain angle, in a certain light, could take on the shape of a person. A shape that was not quite there, but that could be seen, if one looked, if one was tired enough to see.

She sat down on the floor next to the bin.

She said, softly, to the pile: *are you me.*

The pile did not answer.

—

On day 16 she reached the last length.

She knew it was the last length before she had drawn it out. She felt, as she pulled it, that the tension inside her had changed — that there was no longer a slow patient release of stored folded material, but a small final resistance, the resistance of a last thing that did not want to leave. She pulled, and the resistance eased, and the last length came free, and she held it in her hands.

It was small. It was no larger than a handkerchief. It was denser than any of the other lengths, and it was dark, almost the color of dried blood, and it had a weight to it that the earlier lengths had not had.

She held it in the candlelight.

She could see, on it, the shape of a face.

Not a face drawn. Not a face embroidered. A face pressed, faintly, into the material, as if a face had been laid against it while it was still soft and had left an impression. She could see the faint shape of the closed eyes, and the small nose, and the mouth, and the small oval of the whole. It was the face of a child.

She looked at the face of the child.

She recognized it.

It was her face at, she thought, perhaps six or seven. She had a photograph, in a box at the bottom of her wardrobe, of herself at that age, and this was the face in the photograph. It was Yui as she had been on the day she had cut open the small dead bird her cat had brought her, on the day her mother had said *what are you doing* in the voice her mother used when she had understood something and did not want to have understood it, on the day Yui had realized, though she had not known she was realizing it, that she was going to have to fold up the child she was and put her somewhere and become, for the rest of her life, someone else.

She held the small dark handkerchief with the child's face pressed into it, and she began, at last, to cry.

She cried for a long time.

She had not cried since her grandfather's funeral, when she had been twelve. She did not cry now the way she had cried then, with the shaking small breaths of a child in a black dress. She cried the way she had wanted to cry, then and every day since, and had not been able to. She cried in her small bathroom at three in the morning, holding a folded piece of herself, and she cried until the candle burned down, and then she sat in the dark and cried some more, and finally she stopped.

She was very tired.

She got up. She went into the bedroom. She turned on the small paper lamp.

She looked at the bin.

—

The bin was empty.

She stood in the doorway of her bedroom, in her old cotton nightgown, holding the small dark handkerchief with the child's face on it, and she looked at the empty bin.

The wet towel was still in it. The lengths of pale skin she had drawn out over sixteen days — all of it, forty meters of it or more, an entire second body's worth — were gone.

She looked around the room.

The room was empty.

She looked at the bed.

There was someone lying on the bed.

She did not scream. She had not screamed, at any point in the sixteen days, and she did not scream now. She stood in the doorway of her own bedroom, holding the handkerchief with the child's face pressed into it, and she looked at the woman lying on her bed.

The woman was her.

Not a reflection. Not a photograph. A woman. Lying on her side on the bed, her hands folded under her cheek, her hair short and three months overgrown, her cotton nightgown identical to the one Yui herself was wearing, her whole shape identical, in every particular, to Yui — except that the woman on the bed had her eyes closed, and was breathing very slowly, and was, undeniably, resting.

She had waited a long time to rest.

Yui stood in the doorway.

She looked at the woman on the bed.

She thought about the small dead bird and the doll and the box of photographs and the pump manuals and her mother's voice at seven saying *what are you doing*, and about every fold she had made in herself in every year since, and about the whole quiet careful woman she had become as a result. She thought about her supervisor and her flat and her small polite life, and about how much of that life had been about not being seen, about not being taken, about not being ended.

She thought about the fact that there was, now, someone else in the world who could be Yui Nakamura for a while.

She thought about the fact that she did not, in this moment, want to be Yui Nakamura for a while.

She walked into the room. She placed the small dark handkerchief with the child's face on it on the pillow beside the sleeping woman. The sleeping woman's breath did not change. Yui touched her own face — the face on the handkerchief, the face pressed into the dark material, the child's face — with the tip of her finger, very gently, in the way she might have touched a photograph in a museum.

Then she went to the wardrobe. She took out her coat. She put on her shoes. She took her keys from the small dish by the door.

She did not take her purse. She did not take her phone. She did not take, from the shelf by the door, the small photograph of her mother that had been there for eleven years.

She turned off the paper lamp.

She left the door of the flat unlocked.

She went down the stairs.

The morning was just beginning outside. The light on the street was the pale grey of early spring, the light of five in the morning in Yokohama in March, and the air was cold and clean, and there was no one on the street, and she stood on the pavement in her coat and her nightgown and she took a breath — a long slow breath, the first breath she had taken in thirty-seven years without something folded pressing against the small hollow of her chest — and she began to walk.

She did not know where she was going.

She had, she thought, all the time in the world to find out.
